claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The starting alloy can be produced by powder metallurgy followed by hot isostatic pressing and annealing while retaining a nanocrystalline structure.
Grain boundaries in unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 serve as nucleation sites for radiation-induced Cr/V-rich precipitation.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 0.5 at% Y during powder blending before consolidation.
Y preferentially segregates to high-energy grain boundaries in the modified alloy.
Y segregation lowers the grain-boundary energy.
Y-decorated grain boundaries impede Cr and V diffusion.
Reduced Cr/V diffusion lowers the number of active nucleation sites for irradiation-induced precipitates.
Y segregation reduces the irradiation-induced clustering and growth of Cr/V-rich precipitates.
The nanocrystalline structure promotes recombination of irradiation-induced point defects.
Enhanced point-defect recombination maintains low irradiation hardening.
At approximately 8 dpa and 300–500 °C, Y modification will reduce the Cr/V-rich precipitate volume fraction by more than 50% relative to the undoped control.
At approximately 8 dpa and 300–500 °C, the Y-modified alloy will exhibit a hardness increase of less than approximately 1–2 GPa relative to its unirradiated baseline.
Y addition will retain microstructural stability under irradiation.
Adding Y through powder blending will improve the alloy's suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops appreciable Cr/V-rich precipitation during irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits only modest irradiation hardening.
The proposed behavior applies to energetic-particle irradiation at 300–500 °C up to approximately 8 dpa.
Departures from the proposed Y content or processing conditions may produce deleterious Y-rich secondary phases.
